brief.head: BS, decoded
brief.text: For years Amit Varma ad­mired Ajay Shah’s mod­esty about his “BS ar­ti­cle”. BS, it turned out, meant *Business Standard*, where Shah has writ­ten a col­umn for thirty years. {127-J02}

brief.head: A dialect with an army
brief.text: There is no rea­son for Hindi to be in­her­ently su­pe­rior to Bhojpuri or Maithili, Amit Varma said: a lan­guage is a di­alect with an army. {127-J14}

brief.head: Malign, and inept too
brief.text: Stretching Hanlon’s razor, Amit Varma said the state should be as­sumed both ma­lign and in­com­pe­tent: in­com­pe­tent be­cause it imag­ines it can do far more than it can. {127-J16}

brief.head: Markets, civilised
brief.text: Markets are not a fea­ture of cap­i­tal­ism but the in­ven­tion of civil­i­sa­tion: Ajay Shah thought it was the Soviet leader Gorbachev who said so. {127-J20}

brief.head: Watchers and doers
brief.text: Amit Varma quoted Neil Simon: the world has watch­ers and doers. He called Ajay Shah a doer, ad­mit­ting he is some­times happy being a watcher him­self. {127-J23}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: How we spend our days, of course, is how we spend our lives.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah share what shaped them
lead.head: Ten lenses, two lives

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 127

body: “You come here for en­light­en­ment, but today we will give you in­ti­macy,” Amit Varma told lis­ten­ers. {127-J01}
In the 127th episode of *Everything is Everything*, he and Ajay Shah each of­fered five frame­works that, look­ing back, had shaped how they think and who they be­came.
It was meant to be recorded be­fore a live Life Lessons au­di­ence in Goa, but it rained, in October.

Shah ex­plained what binds the ten to­gether. Reasoning from first prin­ci­ples, he said, “re­ally is our great­est de­fence against all the bull­shit of the world”, and it needs a tool­kit of basic frame­works. {127-C01}
## How the world works

Varma began with nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, which he said should not be left to bi­ol­ogy classes. Knowing how evo­lu­tion wired us, he ar­gued, helps us de­cide which ten­den­cies to dampen and which to am­plify. {127-C02}

Shah’s first was the les­son he would give his 20-year-old self: the world is com­plex. Randomness, non­lin­ear­ity and in­for­ma­tion scat­tered ev­ery­where make it far harder to un­der­stand and con­trol than we think, he said. {127-C03}

Varma ex­tended that with spon­ta­neous order. Language, com­mon law and above all the econ­omy are shaped from the bot­tom up, with prices serv­ing as the lan­guage through which strangers meet each other’s needs. {127-C04}
## The state and the mar­ket

Shah then turned to the state, which Indians, he said, tend to treat as a benev­o­lent mother. He cor­rected that with Max Weber’s def­i­ni­tion of the state as a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence, and with pub­lic choice the­ory: the peo­ple who run it pur­sue their own goals. {127-C05}
Varma’s next frame­work was the dou­ble thank-you mo­ment. When buyer and seller thank each other, both are bet­ter off, and every vol­un­tary ex­change adds to human wel­fare. {127-C06}

Shah’s de­fence against the co­er­cive state was rule of law, which at its core means tak­ing dis­cre­tion away from civil ser­vants: over what is a crime, whom to in­ves­ti­gate and whom to pros­e­cute. {127-C07}
Varma added a bonus from Francis Fukuyama. The Indian state does many things badly, he said, when it should do a few things well, be­gin­ning with rule of law. {127-C08}
## How to live

The last frame­works turned in­ward. Varma’s, taken from a chess grand­mas­ter, is “I play to play”: work for the beauty of it, not the out­come. Even Sisyphus can be happy, he ar­gued, if the point of rolling the rock is to roll the rock. {127-C09}
Desires bor­rowed from oth­ers are thin, he said; the ones truly your own are thick. {127-C10}
Shah’s slo­gan was that life is not a spec­ta­tor sport. “I’d rather play my own shitty cricket,” he said, than watch the world’s he­roes play. {127-C11}
Varma, who quotes Annie Dillard so often that peo­ple joke about it, said a life is an ac­cu­mu­la­tion of days, to be lived one at a time. {127-C12}
Shah added that a life­time, set against a com­plex world, is too big to plan and breeds ap­a­thy. {#hundredyears} “A day, on the other hand, is a tan­gi­ble prob­lem,” he said.
His last frame­work was to give un­con­di­tion­ally, with­out keep­ing score of favours. Giving, he said, makes us hap­pier and frees the mind. {127-C13}
Varma, who has known Shah for many years, vouched for him. “In this par­tic­u­lar case, do as he does, he’s ac­tu­ally done it,” he told lis­ten­ers. {127-S08}
Then the two headed off to­gether, Shah lead­ing so that, Varma ex­plained, any ob­sta­cles would meet him first. {127-J08}

second.label: Heart or cosmos
second.head: Quasar beats the heart
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s genie test splits the hosts between people and physics

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on a quasar or the human heart

body: Amit Varma was ex­plain­ing why the mys­ter­ies of human na­ture move him more than sci­ence when Ajay Shah burst out laugh­ing. Shah had a ques­tion: if a genie of­fered a win­dow into the human heart or one into a quasar fifty mil­lion light years away, which would Varma pick? {#quasar}

Varma chose the human heart, even though, he said, the quasar some­times seems eas­ier to grok. Shah did not hes­i­tate. Give him two neu­tron stars about to crash, a cam­era on the scene and an ob­ser­va­tory full of in­stru­ments, and he would take it any day. {127-S02}
Varma ad­dressed the lis­ten­ers: “Ladies, this is Ajay Shah. This is why he doesn’t ask you ques­tions and lis­ten well. He’s think­ing of quasars.” {#ladies}

quote.text: Let me build a whole ob­ser­va­tory with in­stru­ments there. I take it any day.

third.head: Failure, the lucky break

pic.caption: Amit Varma on failing all his life

body: Amit Varma counts his years of fail­ure as his good for­tune. Responding to Ajay Shah’s les­son that the world is com­plex, he said hu­mil­ity was the qual­ity he was glad­dest to have found, if a lit­tle late in life.

“I think when I was an ar­ro­gant young man who knew noth­ing, the worst thing that could have hap­pened to me is had I suc­ceeded,” he said. Success, a mat­ter of luck, would have made him think him­self great, and he would have stopped learn­ing. {127-S01}
People some­times hear his line “I failed all my life” as Bengali self-pity, he said. He calls it a bless­ing. {#blessing}
Those years, he said, taught him hu­mil­ity, “the only path to growth”, and to ap­pre­ci­ate the com­plex­ity of other human be­ings, mak­ing him more em­pa­thetic.

p2.title: Ten frameworks
p2.deck: Five each from Amit Varma and Ajay Shah: the ideas that shaped how they see the world

quote.text: Once you un­der­stand the ways in which you’re wired, you can fig­ure out what you want to mit­i­gate and what you want to am­plify.

box.title: Five each, ten in all
box.text: Amit Varma: nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, spon­ta­neous order, the dou­ble thank-you mo­ment, play­ing to play, and how we spend our days. Ajay Shah: com­plex­ity, dis­trust of the state, rule of law, doing over watch­ing, and giv­ing un­con­di­tion­ally. Together, a tool­kit for first prin­ci­ples think­ing. {127-C01}

sections.label: Framework 1
sections.head: The awe of understanding
sections.caption: natural selection
body: Amit Varma’s first frame­work was nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, and he ar­gued that it is not a sub­ject that should only be taught in bi­ol­ogy classes.

He dis­cov­ered it through pop­u­lar sci­ence writ­ing: Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate*, then Richard Dawkins’s *The Selfish Gene* and *The Blind Watchmaker*, and Daniel Dennett’s *Consciousness Explained*. {127-R01}
His rea­son for car­ing went back to the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and its in­junc­tion, “Know thy­self.” To make the most of our­selves, he said, we must un­der­stand our­selves.
Varma said he is far more drawn than Ajay Shah to fic­tion and the arts. The great­est mys­ter­ies for him are those of human na­ture: why we love, why we cry, why we feel lonely.
Natural se­lec­tion, he said, helps us come to terms with these puz­zles. Once you un­der­stand how you are wired, you can de­cide what to mit­i­gate and what to am­plify. {127-C02}
## Firmer in his athe­ism

Varma was an athe­ist long be­fore he met the the­ory, and the hosts have an episode ar­gu­ing that athe­ism is less a sys­tem of be­lief than a non-belief. Natural se­lec­tion, he said, so­lid­i­fied it.

He read out Douglas Adams, who wrote that the awe nat­u­ral se­lec­tion in­spired in him made re­li­gious awe seem silly: “I take the awe of un­der­stand­ing over the awe of ig­no­rance any day.” {127-J10}
~ Two episodes on evo­lu­tion had pre­ceded this one, he noted, and an­other, on evo­lu­tion in a larger con­text, was to come.

quote.text: Once you un­der­stand the ways in which you’re wired, you can fig­ure out what you want to mit­i­gate and what you want to am­plify.

sections.label: Framework 2
sections.head: Nobody has the whole jigsaw
sections.caption: why the world is complex
body: If Ajay Shah could say one thing to him­self at 20, it would be that the world is com­plex. It has taken him all the years since to un­der­stand it. {#age20}

He gave three rea­sons. The first is ran­dom­ness. Our tidy sto­ries about the past see only the lottery’s out­come. The Battle of Stalingrad was no done deal, he said, so any anal­ogy to it is sus­pect. {#stalingrad}
The sec­ond is non­lin­ear­ity: small changes can gen­er­ate large changes deep in the fu­ture.

The third is that in­for­ma­tion is spread ev­ery­where. Each cube of air obeys the Navier-Stokes equa­tions, but good weather fore­casts would need a ridicu­lous amount of data. Together, he said, these should make us take three steps back. {127-C03}
## The hum­ble firm
Inside a firm, that means hu­mil­ity: man­age­ment should not imag­ine it knows ev­ery­thing, when tens of thou­sands of em­ploy­ees each hold lit­tle bits of in­for­ma­tion.

The op­po­site is ar­ro­gance. If you are so fatu­ous as to be­lieve that you know, he said, “go build a China model and see how badly that works out”, point­ing to Dan Wang’s re­cent book on the engineer’s view of the world. {127-J12}
~ The in­for­ma­tion no­body has lies in every sin­gle human being, Shah said, so good so­ci­eties and or­gan­i­sa­tions are those that get peo­ple to come forth with it. {#everyhuman}

quote.text: The world is more dif­fi­cult to com­pre­hend and con­trol than we think.

sections.label: Framework 3
sections.head: No committee for language
sections.caption: spontaneous order
body: We are hard­wired to treat every prob­lem as an en­gi­neer­ing prob­lem, Amit Varma said: if a coun­try isn’t run­ning well, find the leader who will fix it. That in­stinct served hunter-gatherer tribes, but it is “pro­foundly against the re­al­ity of the world”.
The episode’s third frame­work was spon­ta­neous order: things that are, in Adam Ferguson’s phrase, “the re­sult of human ac­tion, but not human de­sign”. {127-J13}
Matt Ridley’s *The Evolution of Everything* finds it in nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage, the econ­omy, cul­tural norms and com­mon law.

No cen­tral com­mit­tee de­cides how a lan­guage evolves. Travel through India, Varma said, and every few miles the di­alect changes, each recog­nis­able to the next vil­lage, until it has be­come some­thing else en­tirely. {#village}
## Prices that talk

The most spec­tac­u­lar case, for him, is the econ­omy, as de­scribed in Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*. Prices tell oth­ers what we want and what we lack, so that strangers a thou­sand miles apart can meet each other’s needs. {127-R08}
“This is sound­ing so sen­su­ous al­ready,” he ad­mit­ted. {127-J05}
~ Asked by a com­menter to ex­plain spon­ta­neous order, Varma sug­gested read­ing Ridley, then ask­ing GPT 5 for ex­am­ples and dig­ging deep into each. {#gpt}

quote.text: People don’t re­alise that ac­tu­ally prices are a lan­guage. Prices are how we speak to each other.

sections.label: Frameworks 4 and 6
sections.head: The only gunda on the block
sections.caption: the state and the rule of law
body: Most of us are brought up to see the state as a benev­o­lent mother, or a bit of an NGO, Ajay Shah said. Over the years he came to see this as “a wrong way of think­ing”.

Max Weber sup­plied the first cor­rec­tion: the state is a com­mu­nity that achieves and main­tains a mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence over a given ter­ri­tory. It is, in Shah’s words, “the only gunda on the block”. {127-J15}

Public choice the­ory sup­plied the sec­ond. The peo­ple who staff the state pur­sue their own goals, and those are not the wel­fare of the peo­ple. Amit Varma added his the­sis that every state, with time, turns preda­tory. {#buchanan}
Had Shah, after years in “the belly of the beast”, al­ways seen it this way? “It took me all my life to get these things deeply,” he replied. {127-S07}
## Written in black and white

His de­fence against tyranny was rule of law: an elected leg­is­la­ture writes com­pact, know­able laws, the ex­ec­u­tive only in­ves­ti­gates, and only an in­de­pen­dent judge can sen­tence. Fifty-thousand-word laws and se­lec­tive en­force­ment, he warned, let the gov­ern­ment find some­thing on who­ever it goes after. {#fiftyk}
~ Varma, cit­ing Francis Fukuyama, wants an Indian state that does a few things well, be­gin­ning with rule of law. {127-C08}

quote.text: Rule of law is our only hope, is our only de­fence against the in­evitable pro­gres­sion of co­er­cive power into tyranny.

sections.label: Framework 5
sections.head: Two thank-yous, one coffee
sections.caption: the double thank-you moment
body: Ask for a cof­fee at a cafe, Amit Varma said, and you say thank you when the cup is handed over, and the per­son be­hind the counter says thank you when you pay. {#coffee}

This is the dou­ble thank-you mo­ment, from an ar­ti­cle John Stossel wrote fif­teen or twenty years ago. Varma, who writes about mar­kets all the time, said he has never man­aged one piece that ex­plains their magic so fun­da­men­tally. {#stossel}

Each side val­ues what it re­ceives more than what it gives up, so both are bet­ter off. Our in­stincts, formed when an extra leg of lamb for one hunter meant less for an­other, are zero sum. Voluntary ex­change is pos­i­tive sum. {127-C06}
## Profit as phi­lan­thropy

The Angus Maddison graph of human wel­fare is flat until the 18th or 19th cen­tury, then ex­plodes up­wards. Technology ex­plains part of it, Varma said, but much of it is the spread of mar­kets, with more and more peo­ple to trade with. {#maddison}
He once wrote a col­umn ar­gu­ing that profit is the great­est phi­lan­thropy: there is no bet­ter way to make some­one bet­ter off than by prof­it­ing from a vol­un­tary ex­change.

~ He has ar­gued with Rohini Nilekani against the tri­chotomy of state, so­ci­ety and mar­kets. Markets, he said, are a mech­a­nism through which peo­ple in so­ci­ety ful­fil each other’s needs. {127-J19}

quote.text: The way to max­imise human wel­fare is to max­imise dou­ble thank you mo­ments.

sections.label: Framework 10
sections.head: Generosity without a ledger
sections.caption: giving unconditionally
body: Too many peo­ple, Ajay Shah said, are doing a hus­tle: trad­ing favours, keep­ing IOUs and ex­tract­ing bet­ter terms from the world as they climb a lad­der. He gets it, he said; there is a part of that in every life.
His last frame­work was the al­ter­na­tive: “Why bother? Why keep track? Why keep ac­counts? Why keep score? Just give un­con­di­tion­ally.” {#scorekeeping}

Monitoring who owes what, he said, re­flects fear, in­se­cu­rity and a scarcity mind­set. Giving re­flects abun­dance, and it is in our self-interest: it makes us hap­pier and saves the men­tal band­width spent on keep­ing score. {127-C13}
Freed from the ledger, you get to think about truth and beauty, he said, and some peo­ple will come back to you with “sense­less acts of kind­ness and ir­ra­tional acts of beauty”.
## A friend’s tes­ti­mony
Amit Varma, who has known Shah for many years, said he has been a ben­e­fi­ciary of that giv­ing him­self. {127-S08}
He then made what he called a vo­cif­er­ous de­mand: gen­eros­ity must ex­tend to rec­om­men­da­tions. {127-J07}

~ Shah obliged with Dario Amodei’s essay *Machines of Loving Grace*, on what hap­pens as AI pro­gresses. He is no booster of tech­no­log­i­cal par­adises, he said, but finds it sen­si­ble and thought­ful. {127-R18}

quote.text: And ul­ti­mately life is not about pros­per­ing, it is about flour­ish­ing.
Happiness is you are in this mo­ment. You are with this friend, you share an in­ter­est­ing thought. He cracks a joke. You don’t get the joke. You laugh any­way. That is a mo­ment.

p3.title: Tales from the toolkit
p3.deck: A grandmaster’s riddle, a borrowed want, a happy reinvention and a free day

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s life philosophy, borrowed from a chessboard
stories.head: Not to win, not to draw
body: In the last round of a chess tour­na­ment, the Soviet grand­mas­ter Tigran Petrosian faced an op­po­nent who wanted a draw. Petrosian grew deaf over time, Amit Varma noted, though that played no part in this con­ver­sa­tion.
Hoping Petrosian wanted a draw too, the op­po­nent leaned for­ward at one point and whis­pered: “Are you play­ing to win?” Petrosian shook his head.
Our man was hope­ful. A cou­ple of moves later he leaned for­ward again. “Are you play­ing to draw then?” Again Petrosian said no.
Now the op­po­nent was con­fused. If Petrosian was play­ing nei­ther to win nor to draw, why was he play­ing at all? So he asked. “I’m play­ing to play,” Petrosian replied. {127-S03}

Varma loved the story. He wrote a news­let­ter post about it. {127-R14} It has be­come the phi­los­o­phy of his life, and his ad­vice to every young per­son he speaks to: don’t play to win, don’t think of out­comes or grand goals, play for the beauty of it.

One lis­tener had “I play to play” tat­tooed on his arm. Varma was “ob­vi­ously very moved”, he said, though, being a lit­tle old-fashioned, he also won­dered why any­one would mu­ti­late the body. {#tattoo}

~ He reads the myth of Sisyphus the same way. Rolling a rock up a hill for­ever is fu­tile only if the point is to get it to the top, he said. If the point is the rolling it­self, that is your dharma, and you can be happy. {127-C09}
stories.why: Play for a win and the work be­comes a means to an end, and any win soon be­comes the new base­line. Play for its own sake and the joy is in the doing. {#joy}
stories.postscript: Sisyphus came up, Varma said, in his con­ver­sa­tion with Gurcharan Das on *The Seen and the Unseen*.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Tigran Petrosian’s reply

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on where our wants come from
stories.head: Wanting what they want
body: As a young man, the philoso­pher René Girard was asked to teach a lit­er­a­ture course. He needed the extra pocket money, so he agreed, and com­piled a read­ing list of the clas­sics. {127-S04}

Then he re­alised some­thing. In all of those clas­sics, Amit Varma said, “all the he­roes and hero­ines they want some­thing be­cause some­body else wants that thing.” Girard called it mimetic de­sire.

Luke Burgis’s *Wanting* later built on the idea to sep­a­rate thick de­sires from thin ones. Thin de­sires are bor­rowed in search of val­i­da­tion: a young man want­ing a Mercedes, or to be vice pres­i­dent. {#mercedes}

~ Thick de­sires are in­trin­sic, and can be so deep that you are not aware of them. Writing to win the Booker Prize is a thin de­sire, Varma said; writ­ing for the magic of fill­ing a blank page is a thick one. {127-C10}
stories.why: Girard’s idea came out of a side job taken for pocket money. Its les­son is per­sonal: many of our wants are bor­rowed, and it takes a long time, Varma said, to get to the ones that are truly ours. {#thick}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on René Girard’s reading list

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the pleasures of the research life
stories.head: Reinventing the wheel, happily
body: Ajay Shah has a story from his life in re­search, one he has started to see hap­pen to many other peo­ple. His ex­cite­ment is in doing re­search; read­ing pa­pers is only a means to that end.

Very often, he said, he ends up rein­vent­ing from scratch some­thing that oth­ers have al­ready done. And that is okay. If the pur­pose is the joy of doing, you are happy; if it is a pub­li­ca­tion or a patent, you are un­happy. {127-S05}
He still reads other peo­ple, be­cause it jogs the mind. But the pri­mal plea­sure, he said, lies in com­ing up with ideas and in­vent­ing things.
~ It fits his slo­gan that life is not a spec­ta­tor sport. Doing things your­self, he said, is a hun­dred times more ex­cit­ing than watch­ing oth­ers do them. {#hundredx}

quote.text: You turn the key and the door opens and you see things that have never been seen be­fore

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on reinventing what others found

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on living Annie Dillard’s line
stories.head: Master of his own time
body: Amit Varma has not had a full-time job for sev­en­teen or eigh­teen years. The rea­son, he said, is that he wants to be the mas­ter of his own time. {127-S06}

As a young man he as­pired to great­ness: to write great books, make great movies, think great thoughts. The dan­ger, he said, is that every day be­comes a wait­ing room for a glo­ri­ous fu­ture. {127-C12}

Now he wants to wake up look­ing for­ward to the day. He was happy, he said, with how he spent the day of the record­ing: shoot­ing with Ajay Shah, chat­ting, doing matar­gashti, “one of the great terms of our times”. {127-J25}
~ Happiness, he said, is not a mem­ory of a time you think you must have been happy. It is being in the mo­ment with a friend who cracks a joke you don’t get, and laugh­ing any­way. {#happiness}
stories.why: If life is an ac­cu­mu­la­tion of days, a good day mat­ters more than an im­pres­sive ca­reer. Ajay Shah’s ad­di­tion: a life­time is too big to plan, but a day is a prob­lem you can act on. {#agency}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on being master of his own time

words in a law, long enough that or­di­nary life means break­ing it

years, or eigh­teen, that Amit Varma has gone with­out a full-time job

overheard.text: I’m like yeah in mul­ti­ple ways, but how did you know? We con­tain mul­ti­tudes of sick, right?
overheard.who: Amit Varma, on Gen Z calling him sick

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah mean for years when he said he had written a “BS article”?
quiz.a: A col­umn for the *Business Standard*, where he has writ­ten for thirty years.

quiz.q: Offered a window into the human heart or a distant quasar, which did each host choose?
quiz.a: Amit Varma chose the human heart; Ajay Shah chose the quasar with­out hes­i­tat­ing.

quiz.q: Whose definition of the state as a monopoly of physical violence did Ajay Shah use?
quiz.a: Max Weber’s, which led Shah to call the state the only gunda on the block.

quiz.q: When you buy a coffee, why do both you and the seller say thank you?
quiz.a: Each val­ues what they re­ceive more than what they give: a dou­ble thank-you mo­ment.

quiz.q: What did Tigran Petrosian say when asked why he was playing, if not to win or draw?
quiz.a: “I’m play­ing to play,” a line Amit Varma made his life phi­los­o­phy.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, what is life about, if not prospering?
quiz.a: Flourishing, he said, while mak­ing the case for giv­ing un­con­di­tion­ally.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 127. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Richard Dawkins (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0); Douglas Adams (Michael Hughes, CC BY-SA 2.0); Adam Ferguson (Joshua Reynolds, public domain); Max Weber (Ernst Gottmann, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0).

shelf.title: The Blank Slate
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: Amit’s gate­way into nat­u­ral se­lec­tion and evo­lu­tion­ary psy­chol­ogy: Pinker ex­am­ines human na­ture and so­ci­ety through our evo­lu­tion­ary hard­wiring.

shelf.title: The Selfish Gene
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s metaphor of the self­ish gene which, read care­fully rather than lit­er­ally, ex­plains why hu­mans are ca­pa­ble of love and al­tru­ism.

shelf.title: The Blind Watchmaker
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins shows how in­tri­cate de­sign, like the eye, arises with­out a de­signer: the bi­o­log­i­cal coun­ter­part of Hayek’s point about economies.

shelf.title: Consciousness Explained
shelf.creator: Daniel Dennett
shelf.why: It helped him apply evo­lu­tion­ary think­ing to the mys­ter­ies of the mind and human na­ture.

shelf.title: Every Grain of Sand
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: A beau­ti­ful Dylan lyric about our place in the nat­u­ral order, ‘like every spar­row fall­ing, like every grain of sand’, which Amit uses for the idea that the an­swers are dis­trib­uted all around us.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley finds the same bot­tom-up process, with no plan­ner or de­signer, be­hind nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage, prices, cul­tural norms and com­mon law.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything — Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen (with Matt Ridley)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Matt Ridley, a com­pan­ion to his book, on how order emerges bot­tom-up with­out cen­tral de­sign, across bi­ol­ogy, cul­ture and mar­kets.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: Profit = Philanthropy
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that in a world of vol­un­tary ex­change the only way to profit is by mak­ing some­one else bet­ter off, which makes profit an in­cen­tive to do good and the high­est form of phi­lan­thropy.

shelf.title: Rohini Nilekani Pays It Forward — Episode 317 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Rohini Nilekani’s frame­work of so­ci­ety, state and mar­kets as sep­a­rate pil­lars, which Amit cri­tiques: he sees mar­kets as a mech­a­nism through which so­ci­ety meets its own needs by vol­un­tary co­op­er­a­tion.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episodes on the state (Episodes 25 and 26, and the public choice theory episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: State Building
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: A slim book that re­places the vague ‘big state ver­sus small state’ de­bate with two di­men­sions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it.

shelf.title: I Play to Play
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s essay on the phi­los­o­phy that guides his life and that he gives every young per­son he ad­vises: the game it­self, not win­ning, is the re­ward.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Gurcharan Das — Episode 425 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Gurcharan Das’s first-hand sto­ries of sell­ing re­form and of cor­po­rate nim­ble­ness; the con­ver­sa­tion led Amit to reread Sisyphus as a story about find­ing mean­ing in the act it­self rather than fu­til­ity.

shelf.title: Wanting
shelf.creator: Luke Burgis
shelf.why: Burgis brings René Girard’s mimetic de­sire into ev­ery­day life: we want things be­cause oth­ers want them.

shelf.title: Collected Poems
shelf.creator: Mark Strand
shelf.why: Strand is his favourite poet of all time.

shelf.title: Machines of Loving Grace
shelf.creator: Dario Amodei
shelf.why: Ajay is no ‘rah-rah’ booster of tech par­adises, but he finds this essay sen­si­ble and thought­ful about what hap­pens as AI pro­gresses, and says ev­ery­one should read it.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Amit opens: ‘You come here for en­light­en­ment, but today we will give you in­ti­macy.’ The episode was meant to be shot be­fore a live Life Lessons au­di­ence in Goa, but ‘It rained in Goa in October, who would have thought?’
For years Amit heard Ajay say he’d ‘just writ­ten a BS article’ and ad­mired the ex­treme mod­esty. Then he re­alised BS meant Business Standard, where Ajay has had a col­umn for thirty years.

When Ajay laughs mid-monologue, Amit asks: ‘Am I so deeply at­trac­tive that you can’t just help burst out with hap­pi­ness?’ After Ajay picks the quasar over the human heart, Amit adds: ‘Ladies, this is Ajay Shah. This is why he doesn’t ask you ques­tions and lis­ten well. He’s think­ing of quasars.’
Explaining prices as a lan­guage through which dis­tant strangers ful­fil each other’s needs and make each other happy, Amit stops him­self: ‘This is sound­ing so sen­su­ous al­ready.’

On the lis­tener who had ‘I play to play’ tat­tooed on his arm, Amit was ‘ob­vi­ously very moved’, but also couldn’t help a ‘why body mu­ti­la­tion?’ re­ac­tion, ad­mit­ting he’s ‘a lit­tle old fash­ioned that way.’
Amit’s ‘vo­cif­er­ous demand’: since Ajay preaches gen­eros­ity, ‘you also have to be gen­er­ous with your fuck­ing rec­om­men­da­tions.’

Heading off at the end, Amit tells Ajay to lead ‘partly to make sure that any ob­sta­cles on the path are en­coun­tered by you first and I can craftily avoid them.’ Ajay replies: ‘I’ll clear all the spi­der webs as we pass.’
Douglas Adams on nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, read by Amit: ‘I take the awe of un­der­stand­ing over the awe of ig­no­rance any day.’
‘A lan­guage is a di­alect with an army.’ Amit uses it to argue that Hindi isn’t in­her­ently su­pe­rior to Bhojpuri or Maithili, and notes how pol­i­tics split Hindustani into Hindi and Urdu.
Max Weber’s def­i­ni­tion of the state as a com­mu­nity hold­ing a mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence over a ter­ri­tory, which Ajay calls ‘the only gunda on the block’.
Gorbachev, quoted by Ajay: ‘mar­kets are not a fea­ture of cap­i­tal­ism, mar­kets are the in­ven­tion of civ­i­liza­tion.’
Annie Dillard: ‘How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.’
